title: Pauri 32, sound: ik doo jeebhau
tomorrow: Pauri 32, meaning: the steps of the ladder

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pauri 31, the storehouses in every world. Your line was filled once, for all. Did you stop once and look at what was already on your shelf? Today, a new part of the Japji begins. Day two hundred sixteen.

Listen to a small child tell a parent how much they love them. I love you a hundred. No, a thousand. No, a million, a billion, infinity. Infinity plus one. The numbers keep climbing because the feeling is bigger than any number they know. Grown-ups smile, but the child has found something true: when love runs past what you can say, you reach for the biggest counting word there is, and then you go past it. Guru Nanak does something like this in Pauri 32, with a tongue instead of a number. It's the first stanza of a new stretch of Japji, the ladder and the realms. Today, how it sounds.
screen: `I LOVE YOU A MILLION.` → `INFINITY PLUS ONE.` → `A TONGUE INSTEAD OF A NUMBER.`

segments.voice: Here is the opening of Pauri 32: ik doo jeebhau lakh hohi, lakh hoveh lakh vees. Take it apart. Ik: one. Doo: from, out of. Jeebhau: tongue. So ik doo jeebhau: from one tongue. Lakh: a hundred thousand. In South Asia people still count in lakhs, the way Americans count in thousands. Hohi: become. From one tongue, let there be a hundred thousand. And then Nanak goes past it. Lakh hoveh lakh vees: and let those hundred thousand become twenty times a hundred thousand. That's two million tongues. It's the child's infinity plus one, in the language of a poet. Now listen to the music. Ik doo jeebhau: three light steps, then a vowel that opens, jee-bhau. Lakh hohi: short and hard. Then lakh hoveh lakh vees, where lakh sounds twice, like a drumbeat getting faster. You can hear the numbers pile up. What will all those tongues do? That's tomorrow, along with a word that tells you where this stanza is going. For today, notice what kind of wish this is. It isn't a wish for more money, or more time, or more of anything for oneself. It's a wish for more ways to say one thing. Hold on to that wish; the next stanzas climb from it.
screen: `IK DOO JEEBHAU — FROM ONE TONGUE.` · `LAKH HOHI — A HUNDRED THOUSAND.` · `LAKH VEES — TWENTY TIMES MORE.` · `A WISH FOR MORE WAYS TO SAY IT.` · then, large: `IK DOO JEEBHAU.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud, slowly: ik doo jeebhau lakh hohi, lakh hoveh lakh vees. Say it three times, and let the lakh land like a drumbeat each time. Then close your mouth and let the tongue rest, soft, behind your teeth. Feel it there, one tongue, doing nothing. Breathe through your nose and stay with that quiet. If a thought comes, let it pass without saying it. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 32. It opens with a wish: from one tongue, a hundred thousand, and then two million. The first stanza of the ladder.
Your line: ik doo jeebhau, from one tongue. Today, before you speak in a hard moment, notice your one tongue, and choose one good thing to say with it. Day two hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 32 opens the stretch many teachers call the ladder and the realms, and it opens with the image of a single tongue multiplied into two million.

original.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 32: from one tongue, let there be a hundred thousand.

trapdoor: what you thought: someone wants to talk a lot.
what it means: a longing so large that one tongue isn't enough to say the One's Name.
what a scholar hears: lakh vees is twenty lakh, two million; the stanza opens the part of Japji many teachers call the ladder and the realms.
